---
title: "Real Data Case 1: Wage Determination"
number-sections: true
---

## Research Question

How do education and labor market experience affect wages?
This chapter illustrates how standard econometric issues arise in real data and how appropriate modeling choices improve inference.

## Data Description

We use the `wage1` dataset from the `wooldridge` package.
The data are a cross-section of individuals and include information on hourly wages, education, and labor market experience.

```{r}
library(wooldridge)
data(wage1)

summary(wage1[, c("wage", "educ", "exper", "tenure")])
```

## Naive OLS in Levels

We begin with a simple linear regression of wages on years of education.

```{r}
ols_levels <- lm(wage ~ educ, data = wage1)
summary(ols_levels)
```

While the estimated coefficient on education is positive, this specification is problematic due to the strong right skewness of wages and non-constant variance.

## Functional Form: Log Wages

A standard transformation is to model the logarithm of wages.

```{r}
ols_log <- lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper + I(exper^2), data = wage1)
summary(ols_log)
```

In this specification, the coefficient on education can be interpreted as the approximate percentage increase in wages associated with an additional year of schooling.

## Heteroskedasticity

We examine residuals from the log-wage regression.

```{r}
plot(fitted(ols_log), resid(ols_log),
     xlab = "Fitted values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs Fitted Values")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")
```

Although the log transformation reduces heteroskedasticity, some variance heterogeneity remains.

## Robust Inference

We compare classical and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.

```{r}
X <- model.matrix(ols_log)
u <- resid(ols_log)
XtX_inv <- solve(crossprod(X))

meat_white <- crossprod(X * u)
vcov_white <- XtX_inv %*% meat_white %*% XtX_inv

se_classical <- summary(ols_log)$coefficients[, "Std. Error"]
se_robust <- sqrt(diag(vcov_white))

se_table <- data.frame(
  Classical_SE = round(se_classical, 4),
  Robust_SE = round(se_robust, 4)
)

knitr::kable(
  se_table,
  caption = "Classical and Robust Standard Errors"
)
```

Robust standard errors are slightly larger, indicating that classical inference may understate uncertainty.

## Lessons Learned

- Functional form choices have substantial implications for interpretation and inference.
- Log transformations often stabilize variance in wage regressions.
- Heteroskedasticity is pervasive in cross-sectional data.
- Robust standard errors should be standard practice in applied work.
